extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or beginning graduate students in measure theory and probability (and instructors)
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter excerpt containing definitions, theorems, proofs, and exercises on product measures, Fubini's theorem, independence, convolutions, and related probabilistic inequalities; intended as textbook material and problem set for measure-theoretic probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jensen's inequality (multivariate form)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ : R^n → R is convex and X = (X1,...,Xn) is a random vector with E|φ(X)| < ∞ and E|Xi| < ∞ for all i, then E φ(X1,...,Xn) ≥ φ(EX1,...,EXn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise asks to imitate proof of single-variable Jensen (Theorem 1.5.1). The condition requires integrability of φ(X) and each Xi. Use convexity and linearity of expectation; equality conditions appear in earlier discussion (e.g., when φ(EX)=Eφ(X) implies a.s. constancy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chebyshev inequality sharpness and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Chebyshev's inequality can be sharp in some cases and not sharp in others: (i) for fixed 0 < b ≤ a there exists X with EX^2 = b^2 such that P(|X| ≥ a) = b^2/a^2; (ii) if 0 < EX^2 < ∞ then a^2 P(|X| ≥ a)/EX^2 → 0 as a → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise demonstrates both attainability of the bound in finite cases and that the Chebyshev bound becomes trivial at infinity when second moment finite; construct discrete examples for (i) and use tail behavior for (ii).

rubrics_metrics.name: One-sided Chebyshev bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a > b > 0 and a two-point distribution P(X=a)=p, P(X=-b)=1-p, applying Chebyshev to φ(x)=(x+b)^2 shows that among all Y with the same mean and variance as X, P(Y ≥ a) ≤ p, with equality when Y=X. Also, for EY=0, var(Y)=σ^2, P(Y ≥ a) ≤ σ^2/(a^2+σ^2) and equality is attained for some Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Chebyshev/Chebyshev-like inequality on shifted square and optimize; construct extremal two-point distributions to show equality cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonexistence of certain positive lower bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: For specified parameters, infimums of probabilities over distributions with given moments can be zero: (i) for ε>0, inf{P(|X|>ε): EX=0,var(X)=1} = 0. (ii) for y ≥ 1 and σ^2 ∈ (0,∞), inf{P(|X|>y): EX=1,var(X)=σ^2} = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct sequences of distributions concentrating mass so that tail probabilities shrink to zero while preserving prescribed mean and variance; shows there is no uniform positive lower bound under those constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound from Cauchy–Schwarz
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y ≥ 0 with E Y^2 < ∞ then P(Y > 0) ≥ (E Y)^2 / E Y^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to Y·1(Y>0) to obtain the inequality. Useful as a probabilistic lower bound relating mean and second moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominated convergence may fail without domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: on (0,1) with Lebesgue measure, with α ∈ (1,2) and Xn(x) = n^α 1_{(1/(n+1),1/n)}(x), we have Xn → 0 a.s. and Theorem 1.6.8 applies with suitable h and g, but {Xn} are not dominated by an integrable function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise exhibits sequence of functions converging a.s. but without an integrable dominating function, illustrating necessity of domination hypotheses in dominated convergence theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration against absolutely continuous measure
rubrics_metrics.description: If probability measure µ has density f w.r.t. Lebesgue measure (i.e., µ(A)=∫_A f(x) dx), then for any g with g ≥ 0 or ∫|g| dµ < ∞ we have ∫ g dµ = ∫ g(x) f(x) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proof technique of Theorem 1.6.9 (approximation by simple functions, monotone convergence) to transfer integration from µ to Lebesgue measure using density f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion–exclusion formula
rubrics_metrics.description: For events A1,...,An, P(∪_{i=1}^n Ai) = Σ_i P(Ai) − Σ_{i<j} P(Ai∩Aj) + Σ_{i<j<k} P(Ai∩Aj∩Ak) − ... + (−1)^{n−1} P(∩_{i=1}^n Ai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via expanding indicator 1_{∪Ai} = 1 − Π_i (1 − 1_{Ai}) and taking expectations. Exercise also leads to Bonferroni inequalities by truncating sum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bonferroni inequalities (upper/lower bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truncating inclusion–exclusion after an even (resp. odd) number of terms yields a lower (resp. upper) bound for P(∪Ai); particular inequalities include P(∪Ai) ≤ Σ P(Ai) and more refined bounds involving intersections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by comparing truncated alternating sums from inclusion–exclusion; often used for approximations when higher order intersections unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moment interpolation inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: If E|X|^k < ∞ then for 0 < j < k, E|X|^j < ∞ and E|X|^j ≤ (E|X|^k)^{j/k}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard consequence of Hölder/Power mean inequality; exercise asks to show integrability of lower moments and the bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: AM ≥ GM via Jensen
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying Jensen's inequality with φ(x)=e^x to a discrete distribution yields Σ p(m) y_m ≥ Π y_m^{p(m)}, so with uniform weights this is the arithmetic mean ≥ geometric mean inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise demonstrates using convex exponential function and discrete Jensen instance to recover AM≥GM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone convergence for increasing sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: If EX^- < ∞ (?) and Xn ↑ X then EXn ↑ EX (exercise 1.6.13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of monotone convergence theorem to expectations of increasing sequence of nonnegative parts; ensure integrability conditions required in statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing tails for reciprocals
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ≥ 0 but E(1/X) may be infinite, then lim_{y→∞} y E(1/X; X>y) = 0 and lim_{y↓0} y E(1/X; X>y) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises exploring tail integrals for reciprocals; use splitting and bounds to show vanishing behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countable-sum exchange for disjoint sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If X integrable and {An} are disjoint with union A, then Σ_{n=0}^∞ E(X;An) = E(X;A); i.e., the sum converges absolutely and equals the integral over the union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orthogonality of disjoint supports and Fubini/monotone convergence reasoning; used to justify series-integration interchange when supports disjoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and uniqueness of product measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two σ-finite measure spaces (X,A,µ1) and (Y,B,µ2), there is a unique measure µ on the σ-algebra generated by rectangles with µ(A×B)=µ1(A)µ2(B) (notation µ1×µ2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to verifying additivity on disjoint unions of rectangles and uses σ-finiteness; uniqueness follows from Carathéodory’s extension or Theorem 1.1.9. Induction gives product measure for n-fold products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fubini's theorem (iterated integrals equal double integral)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ≥ 0 or ∫|f| dµ < ∞ on X×Y with µ = µ1×µ2 and µ1,µ2 σ-finite, then ∫ f dµ = ∫ (∫ f(x,y) µ2(dy)) µ1(dx) = ∫ (∫ f(x,y) µ1(dx)) µ2(dy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by approximating indicator functions of measurable sets (lemmas on cross-sections), then simple functions, monotone convergence, and decomposition into positive/negative parts. Requires measurability of sections and appropriate integrability or nonnegativity hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurability of cross-sections (Lemma 1.7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E ∈ F (the product σ-algebra) then for each fixed x, Ex = {y : (x,y) ∈ E} ∈ B (is Borel measurable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show collection of E with measurable cross-sections is a σ-algebra containing rectangles, hence all of F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurability and integral identity for section measures (Lemma 1.7.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E ∈ F then g(x) := µ2(Ex) is A-measurable and ∫ g dµ1 = µ(E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove for finite-measure case and extend by σ-finiteness, using Dynkin's π-λ theorem to handle the σ-algebra closure; monotone convergence used for increasing unions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of Fubini hypotheses (counterexamples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show iterated integrals can differ if absolute integrability fails (Example 1.7.5 and 1.7.6), σ-finiteness is necessary (Example 1.7.7), and measurability issues (depending on set-theoretic axioms) can violate expected equalities (Example 1.7.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete constructions provided: a signed grid-sum example giving different row/column sums, exponential kernel with opposite-signed iterated integrals, counting vs Lebesgue measures non-σ-finite mismatch, and a CH/AC-based ordering producing nonmeasurable-like sections; exercise demonstrates what can go wrong if hypotheses dropped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated integral absolute integrability criterion (Exercise 1.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∫_X ∫_Y |f(x,y)| µ2(dy) µ1(dx) < ∞ then the three integrals (iterated and full) exist and are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary and exercises emphasize Fubini's absolute integrability criterion and justify switching sums/integrals under integrability conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-measure representation of area under graph (Exercise 1.7.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For measurable g≥0, ∫_X g dµ = (µ×λ)({(x,y):0≤y<g(x)}) = ∫_0^∞ µ({x:g(x)>y}) dy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Cavalieri principle and Fubini to represent integrals as measures of subgraphs; helpful in measure-transform computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of convolution representation for sum distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y independent with distribution functions F and G, then P(X+Y ≤ z) = ∫ F(z−y) dG(y); equivalently, when densities exist, the density of X+Y is convolution: h(x)=∫ f(x−y) dG(y) and if Y has density g, h(x)=∫ f(x−y) g(y) dy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via indicator h(x,y)=1(x+y≤z) and Theorem 2.1.12 (expectation via product measure); useful for computing sums of independent variables and for known families (gamma, normal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of independence (events, r.v.s, σ-fields)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events A,B independent iff P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). Random variables X,Y independent iff for all Borel sets C,D, P(X∈C,Y∈D)=P(X∈C)P(Y∈D). σ-fields F,G independent iff for all A∈F,B∈G events are independent. Infinite collections independent if every finite subcollection is independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple equivalent formulations (indicator variables, generated σ-fields) are provided; independence of σ-fields implies independence of measurable functions adapted to those σ-fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: π–λ theorem (Dynkin)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is a π-system and L is a λ-system containing P then σ(P) ⊂ L (i.e., the σ-algebra generated by P is contained in L).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tool used to extend properties known on a π-system (e.g., rectangles) to the full σ-algebra; central in proofs about independence extending from generators to generated σ-fields (Theorem 2.1.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of independence from π-systems to σ-fields (Theorem 2.1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A1,...,An are independent collections of sets and each Ai is a π-system, then the generated σ-fields σ(A1),...,σ(An) are independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs λ-system of sets satisfying the desired factorization property and applies π–λ theorem iteratively; key method to show independence need only be checked on generating π-systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient condition for independence via joint CDF factorization (Theorem 2.1.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show X1,...,Xn are independent it suffices that for all real x1,...,xn, P(X1≤x1,...,Xn≤xn) = Π_i P(Xi≤xi) (i.e., joint CDF factors as product of marginals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sets {Xi ≤ xi} as a π-system generating σ(Xi) and apply Theorem 2.1.7; common practical criterion since distribution functions are often known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of independent collections are independent (Theorem 2.1.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for each i the family {Xi,j : 1≤j≤m(i)} are independent across i and fi : R^{m(i)}→R measurable, then fi(Xi,1,...,Xi,m(i)) (one per i) are independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof passes to σ-fields: Fi,j = σ(Xi,j), Gi = σ(∪_j Fi,j) and applies Theorem 2.1.9/2.1.7; used frequently to show combinations (sums, products) of disjoint blocks of independent variables remain independent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product distribution of independent random variables (Theorem 2.1.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X1,...,Xn independent with marginal distributions µi then the joint distribution of (X1,...,Xn) is the product measure µ1×...×µn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check equality on rectangle sets and apply uniqueness via π-system generating R^n; important for constructing multivariate distributions from marginals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation factorization for independent variables (Theorem 2.1.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y independent and h:R^2→R measurable with h≥0 or E|h(X,Y)|<∞ then E h(X,Y) = ∫∫ h(x,y) µ(dx) ν(dy). In particular, if h(x,y)=f(x)g(y) with integrability, then E f(X) g(Y) = E f(X) · E g(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines product-measure representation of joint law with Fubini to factor expectations; apply to prove factorization of moments and independence implications for expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of product equals product of expectations under mild conditions (Theorem 2.1.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X1,...,Xn are independent and either all Xi ≥ 0 or E|Xi|<∞ for each i, then E(Π_i Xi) = Π_i E Xi (i.e., expectation of product equals product of expectations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction and Theorem 2.1.12; verify integrability of partial products via independence and bounds on moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convolution density formula for sum (Theorem 2.1.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X has density f and Y has distribution function G (or density g), independent, then X+Y has density h(x)=∫ f(x−y) dG(y) (or h(x)=∫ f(x−y) g(y) dy when g exists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive from convolution of distribution functions and apply Fubini when integrands nonnegative; used to derive closed forms for sums of common families (gamma, normal, Poisson discrete convolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kolmogorov extension theorem (consistency → product measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given consistent finite-dimensional probability measures µ_n on (R^n,R^n) (consistency: µ_{n+1}(A×R)=µ_n(A) for rectangles), there is a unique probability measure P on (R^N,R^N) assigning those finite-dimensional marginals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides existence of infinite sequences of random variables with prescribed finite-dimensional distributions; requires consistency of the family of finite-dimensional measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard Borel / 'nice' spaces for extension
rubrics_metrics.description: A measurable space (S,S) is 'nice' if there exists a 1-1 measurable map φ : S → R with measurable inverse. Borel subsets of complete separable metric spaces (Polish spaces) are nice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kolmogorov extension generalization to product spaces requires 'nice' (standard Borel) spaces; the textbook outlines constructive maps (e.g., embedding into [0,1)^N via dense sequences) and warns about pathological counterexamples when spaces not nice.
